#6718. Homemade Cranberry Sauce

I don’t care if you love it or hate it—cranberry sauce is a Thanksgiving STAPLE. Personally, I love it. Every year, you can find me spooning multiple helpings of the sweet-tart sauce onto my plate to balance out all of the rich savory dishes. While I understand the nostalgic appeal of the canned stuff, homemade cranberry sauce is 1,000x better. It's fresh, versatile, and so easy to make. All you need are 5 ingredients and 20 minutes to make this staple holiday side.

What People Are Saying:“This is the simplest, but tastiest cranberry sauce i’ve ever made… My family loved it so much, i’ve had to make several batches for christmas gifts, per request.” -OrangeSushi

“Made this for Thanksgiving, and everyone loved it, including the ones that don’t care for cranberry sauce!! I added some fresh mandarin oranges and cinnamon to mine. Everyone wanted leftovers to take home! We put it in our oatmeal with pecans for breakfast in the morning! I plan to make this all year round instead of just at Thanksgiving! ❤️” -RedDice

First, grab a small saucepan—but not just any saucepan! Make sure it’s either stainless steel or enameled cast-iron. Whatever you do, avoid aluminum, which will react with the copious acid in the berries, giving the sauce an unpleasant metallic taste. Add the sugar and 1 c. water and stir until the sugar is dissolved. Now add the cranberries and bring the mixture to a boil over medium-high heat.

The beauty of cranberries is that (1) they readily burst and release their juices, and (2) their juices have so much natural pectin that the berries thicken nearly to jam in mere minutes. Ten minutes of simmering, with some occasional stirring thrown in, is all the cooking required. Don’t sweat it if a small minority of the berries haven’t burst—they probably will by the time the sauce has cooled.

Stir in the orange zest and let the sauce cool; it will continue to thicken. And believe it or not, that really is all there is to it. What’s more, this is a Thanksgiving dish you can get off your plate up to 1 week in advance. Just transfer the cooled cranberry sauce to an airtight container and refrigerate until the big feast. Bonus: The flavors will continue to meld and deepen while it hangs out in the fridge.

The full list of ingredients and directions can be found in the recipe below.

While this version is perfectly classic, if you want to experiment, you’ve got a few options. If your cranberry sauce isn’t complete without orange juice, you can sub freshly squeezed or bottled orange juice for some or all of the water. Alternatively, if you’re averse to oranges, feel free to skip the zest and add a pinch of ground cinnamon or a couple of cinnamon sticks instead. Craving some crunch? Throw in some chopped pecans at the end of cooking.

Check out our keto cranberry sauce if you're looking to satisfy every diet, or our cranberry relish if you want a similar side without having to turn on your stove.

If you have leftovers, store them in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 1 week.

Justin and Hailey Bieber’s son Jack Blues Bieber is only 2, but he’s already getting into music. Hailey posted a rare video of Jack playing the keyboard at home. “Blues loves the keys,” she wrote.

Hailey shed more light on Jack’s interests earlier this year. During her discussion on Therapuss in February, she revealed that Jack was already reciting the lyrics to his dad’s hit song “Baby.”

“He’s been saying, ‘Baby, oh baby, oh baby oh.’ And I’m like, ‘Whoa, that is so crazy,’” she said.

Jack is also drawn to one particular sport: “So he talks a lot about basketball,” Hailey said. “He says ‘basketball’ all the time. Speaking on motherhood more broadly, the model added, “I think it’s just the coolest thing to watch a little person become their own little person. I’m watching him get his personality. I’m seeing what he’s into. He likes basketball. He likes this thing. You know? It’s so fun.”

While Hailey has been open about Jack in interviews, she only shares glimpses of his life on occasion. The model last posted a photo of Jack during Halloween weekend, revealing he dressed up as a ghost.

#6716. Joe Budden Can't Stop Betting on Himself

This is an edition of the weekly newsletter Tap In, GQ senior associate editor Frazier Tharpe’s final word on the most heated online discourse about music, movies, and TV. Sign up here to get it free.

There’s Joe Budden, and then there’s everyone else. Despite the proliferation of rapper-led podcasts and talk shows in the last few years (itself a subset of the ever-ballooning celebrity podcast bubble), there’s no question who leads the pack—at least that’s how Budden sees it. It’s hard to argue with him: in February, Budden’s self-titled and pioneering podcast will turn 12,. Not too long ago, he posted a screenshot that “accidentally” revealed his yearly take-home was a number in the low eight figures.

Through it all, there've been dramatic cast changes, tense moments with rappers, hilarious must-see breakdowns of big moments in culture, and several dust-ups with Drake, a frequent subject of Budden and his co-host’s. Being part-New Jerseyian, I’m one of the vocal minority that believe it’s a travesty to reduce Budden’s rap career to “Pump It Up” (this is never far from my Recently Played to this day). Our paths actually crossed during his time at Complex, when I served as a sit-in for test episodes of Everyday Struggle while he searched for the co-host that would eventually become Akademiks—and even helped them launch the show with a series of digital short skits I wrote and produced that are probably lost to the internet by now.

As an occasional pod listener, I find it fascinating that Budden has defied all odds, and everyone who said he was bound to burn bridges, and now finds himself commanding attention, revenue and even reconciliations with his past employers. Despite how things went with State of the Culture, he’s back in business with Revolt. Joe Budden Network Presents, his new weekly series, premieres on November 13th, bringing his podcast to linear television through a unique micro-licensing partnership that allows Joe to retain full ownership of his IP.

To mark his next chapter, we talked about the current landscape of rap media and podcasting, the dangers of getting too comfortable, and how he plans to maintain his reign.

#6715. Ayo Edebiri Is Electric in a Pinstripe Conner Ives Suit at the 2026 GQ Men of the Year Party

Ayo Edebiri has proven herself to be quite the chameleon on the red carpet. From her cream tank that morphed into a feathery bustle at the BFI London Film Festival last month, to her draping white gown at this year’s Met Gala, Edebiri can pull off almost any look with ease. However, she appears to be following in the footsteps of fashion forebears like Julia Roberts and Diane Keaton, thanks to her particular affinity for suits.

In the past, Edebiri has turned sharp suited looks such as her icy-blue capri set at the Los Angeles premiere of Inside Out 2, and her gray Loewe ensemble at the 2025 Golden Globes, which was notably punctuated with a golden, feather-shaped tie. And it appears she’s still digging through the menswear section—and the results are just as impressive.

On Thursday night in Los Angeles, The Bear star attended the 2026 GQ Men of the Year ceremony, where she wore an eye-popping ensemble pulled from the Conner Ives Spring/Summer 2027 ready-to-wear collection (a choice that, perhaps, served as a nod to the celebrated gentlemen of the evening).

The look consisted of a fitted black blazer and pants, both stitched with a subtle gray pinstripe for a slightly ’80s touch.

Similar to how it debuted on the runway, stylist Danielle Goldberg layered the suit over a seafoam-green dress shirt and a burgundy patterned tie, both visible thanks to the open blazer.

But while the original catwalk fit saw the tie tucked into the pants and cinched under a cummerbund, here, Edebiri went sans the waist accessory, while the necktie hung free.

She accessorized the fit with shiny black loafers and diamond earrings, while her hair was styled in a curly, slicked bob.

Needless to say, this suited realm is clearly where Edebiri thrives.

#6714. ‘Clothing Has Impact’: Zoe Latta, Kat Typaldos, and Turner on Styling Los Angeles Mayor-Elect Nithya Raman

When Nithya Raman stepped onto the podium for her first press conference as the newly minted mayor-elect of Los Angeles, keen eyes might have clocked her “if you know, you know” attire—specifically, a vintage tangerine Narciso Rodriguez motorcycle jacket and a pair of Eckhaus Latta jeans. Throughout much of her political career as a two-term LA councilwoman, Raman has deployed the classic conventions of a local representative—a sturdy button-down shirt here, a matching pantsuit there. Her more fashion-forward transformation in recent months comes courtesy of an unlikely political styling trio: fashion designer Zoe Latta (of bicoastal cool-kid brand Eckhaus Latta) and celebrity stylists Kat Typaldos and Turner.

No matter which way you cut a pantsuit, female politicians are often boxed in by frustrating parameters. Style is confined by reserved silhouettes barely spiced up by the addition of a pussy bow blouse. And while policy is more important than Prada, Latta, Typaldos, and Turner found plenty of ways to change what’s expected of a candidate’s wardrobe. As Typaldos put it candidly: “If one more person says ‘bold, colorful suit’ for a powerful woman, I will throw my computer out of the window.”

Mayor-Elect Nithya Raman at her first press conference post-win in a Narciso Rodriguez leather jacket from The RealReal and Eckhaus Latta jeans

The cohort connected with Raman’s cause via their mutual LA friend Chas McCarty, a restaurateur and man-about-town. Latta says: “It was in the back of Botanica [a local restaurant, where Raman was holding a campaign gathering]. I had my baby with me, and the binky fell out, and Nithya was mid sentence and got up from the table, got under the table, grabbed the binky, continuing to talk about small businesses and handed it to me, and I was just like, This woman has my book—whatever she needs.”

In the weeks following Raman’s surprise bid against incumbent mayor Karen Bass, a wardrobe shift wasn’t exactly at the top of her to-do list. In those early days, Raman wore what Latta affectionately described as “a lot of capes,” but her traditionalism—and prior lack of a styling team—was part of her appeal. “She wasn’t doing anything wrong—she had other things to do,” Latta says. The task at hand: to give her wardrobe a little zhuzh. “She wears clothes really well. It is a treat to get to dress her, and she enjoys it. And that, to me, is so fundamental. It’s not in a peacocking way.”

Voting day: Cleo Camp top, Altuzarra skirt from The RealReal.

Latta, Typaldos, and Turner are all used to working with powerful women, but in a different arena of celebrity. The one thing they did know about dressing a prospective mayor: a subtle, sustainable approach is best. This included plenty of vintage and secondhand shopping from The RealReal, as well as local designers, casually blended with her preexisting wardrobe. Such fashionable thriftiness not only fit Raman’s grounded style but also spoke to the trio’s sensibilities as self-employed small business owners. “I’m thinking about [the client], the context, the world that they live in,” Turner says. “And I think Kat is probably similar in that we’re thinking about how to make them shine in this world. And so you’re taking into consideration who they are, what they are. You’re doing your research.”

Raman at her election party in a plum Erdem from The RealReal

Unsurprisingly, there was no high-glamour, full-look policy here. Instead, they took a little-bit-of-this, little-bit-of-that approach to arrive at their trustworthy results. It could be a white Akris blouse, a plum Erdem dress, or a burnt orange Altuzarra leather skirt paired with a long-sleeve shirt from LA-based designer Cleo Camps. Yes, there were suits, like the one from J.Crew that Raman wore to debate Bass, but all were items a constituent would want in their own workwear closet. “In that process, we watched Nithya develop agency about what to wear and how clothing can empower,” Typaldos says. “For me, what was cool is that she’s such a denim person, and I trust nobody more [than the person] wearing a striped shirt and a denim and a loafer. Clothing has that impact. How can you make it feel like a second skin enough?”

Raman debates the former incumbent mayor Karen Bass in a J.Crew suit.

When it comes to dressing a politician like Raman, unlike a musician or an actress, there’s no calling in favors. The mayor-to-be couldn’t take so much as a friends-and-family discount from Latta’s own brand, nor was she interested in splurging on outlandish pieces. If it were otherwise, fashion would be an even bigger point of contention for opponents looking to undercut her platform. Case in point: Following New York mayor Zohran Mamdani’s inauguration, his wife Rama Duwaji’s borrowed and rented designer items drew much discussion, with their brand names and price tags splashed across rage-bait headlines in the New York Post. In a feature with The Cut published two months later, the fashion credits, rather untraditionally, made it explicit that the clothing was on loan from the designers, despite that being the standard behind-the-scenes editorial procedure.

Latta, Typaldos, and Turner have never worked as a styling trio before. They attribute their banding together in part to Nithya’s community building. “She really does bring people together,” says Turner. “I haven’t worked with another stylist or designer in this capacity, but it was thoroughly enjoyable to be in the presence of powerful women just trying to help another woman rise up. I think it’ll probably be my most important work to date.”

#6713. Safe Word: The Best Jewelry Launches of November 2026

Safe Word is a series highlighting the latest trends in the jewelry market, keeping you up to date on all things that sparkle and shine.

November’s jewelry launches are looking both backward and forward, with designers revisiting their roots, reworking archival ideas, and stepping into entirely new territory. First up, Quentin Jones is taking her surrealist art off the wall and onto the body with ‘Nocturne’, her first jewelry collection; Pomellato reaches back to 1997 to revive “Moneta Orientale” as a colorful modern talisman; David Yurman celebrates the magic of a New York holiday with Michael B. Jordan, Yerin Ha, and Inde Navarrette; Vhernier revisits its iconic “Trottola” design with new proportions and contrasting materials; Di Volpe reinterprets the classic tennis bracelet with customizable gemstones in “DiSegno”; Brent Neale transforms the classic bow into sculptural fine jewelry with “Wrap It Up”; and Kendra Scott launches the new “Kendra Scott Collection,” reimagining her signature Spike motif as a personal talisman. From archival revivals and meaningful motifs to innovative designs and new creative directions, November’s launches prove that sometimes the best way forward starts with looking back. For the rest of the month, we’ve got you covered on all the jewelry-related happenings worth knowing about.

Quentin Jones is taking her art off the wall and onto the body with “Nocturne,” the first jewelry collection from House of Quentin Jones. Following the multidisciplinary artist’s debut of surrealist ceramics and tapestries last year, the new collection transforms recurring gestures and symbols from her work into sculptural collars, cuffs, armbands, pendants, chains, and earrings. Eyes, hands, stars, moons, tears, and knots take shape in silver and gold vermeil alongside freshwater pearls, onyx, opals, jade, glass, and silk tassels, giving the pieces a dreamlike, talismanic quality. Beginning as drawings and hand collages in Jones’s Brooklyn studio, each design carries her surrealist visual language into wearable form, further blurring the line between art, design, and fashion.

Kendra Scott Launches an Eponymous Collection

Kendra Scott is offering a more personal look into her design world with the launch of the “Kendra Scott Collection,” a new line spanning fashion and fine jewelry. Its first edition, “The Spike,” revisits a silhouette the designer has worn throughout her career as a personal symbol of strength, confidence, and conviction. Inspired by nature and the radiance of the night sky, the collection translates the pointed motif into sculptural necklaces, earrings, bracelets, and charms, balancing bold proportions with intricate craftsmanship. Fashion jewelry incorporates tiger’s eye, malachite, and turquoise, while fine jewelry introduces lab-grown diamonds, pavé detailing, labradorite, and lapis. From statement-making links to delicate diamond charms, the collection offers a new interpretation of Scott’s longtime signature, inviting wearers to make the symbol their own.

Alison Lou’s ‘New Wave’ Collection Experiments With New Materials

Alison Lou is entering a new chapter with “New Wave,” a fine jewelry collection that introduces unexpected materials and a fresh approach to the designer’s signature playful aesthetic. Exploring the relationship between movement and form, the collection pairs lightweight titanium and ceramic with lab-grown diamonds, creating fluid, sculptural silhouettes that curve and catch the light. Available in Fig and Denim Blue colorways, the designs include wavy rings, diamond-accented signets, delicate thread necklaces, and statement drop earrings. With its unconventional materials and easy-to-wear designs, “New Wave” brings a new sense of movement to Alison Lou’s everyday jewelry.

Jenny Bird and Emese Gormley Partner on the Anyu Ring

Jenny Bird is expanding her JB FINE collection with a new collaboration featuring lifestyle creator and Lipstick on the Rim podcast host Emese Gormley. Named in honor of Gormley’s mother, the Anyu Ring offers a personal take on the classic signet, featuring three lab-grown baguette diamonds set in 14-karat yellow or white gold. The understated design combines the timeless appeal of a signet ring with a sentimental tribute to family, bringing a new perspective to Bird’s growing fine jewelry offering. Available exclusively on Jenny Bird’s website, the collaboration makes a case for jewelry that feels as meaningful as it looks.

Pomellato Revives Its 1997 Moneta Orientale Pendant as a Colorful Talisman

Pomellato is looking to its archives for its latest good-luck charm. For the newest chapter of “Memorie d’Archivio,” the maison revives Moneta Orientale, a 1997 pendant inspired by the ancient symbolism of a circle surrounding a square, representing the harmony between heaven and earth. Made in 33 stone-and-pavé combinations, the design pairs colorful hard stones including black jade, amazonite, sodalite, rhodochrosite, and labradorite with Pomellato’s signature irregular pavé of diamonds, sapphires, rubies, and more. Offered in two proportions, each pendant transforms the archival motif into a modern talisman for prosperity and protection.

Bibi van der Velden Makes Her High Jewelry Debut With ‘Eclipse’

Bibi van der Velden is entering a new era with “Eclipse,” the designer’s first high jewelry collection and most refined exploration of diamonds to date. Inspired by the fleeting moment when light gives way to darkness, the collection includes two six-piece suites: one in white diamonds and another defined by an ombré of diamonds into gray spinels deepening into black. Van der Velden’s signature alligator motif is abstracted into fluid, sculptural silhouettes, with scales engraved into the white gold on the reverse of each piece. “With Eclipse, I wanted to take those familiar elements and transform them into something more abstract and sculptural,” she says. “It’s a collection about transformation, which has always been at the heart of my work.”

Aflalo and Leandra Medine Cohen Turn Everyday Indulgences Into Fine Jewelry

Aflalo is finding the humor in our obsession with wellness with “The Vanities,” a new two-piece fine jewelry capsule designed exclusively by Leandra Medine Cohen. Playing with the contradiction between longevity and life’s little indulgences, the collection transforms two unlikely everyday accessories into precious objects. The Memento Mori is a 14-karat yellow gold cigar band set with more than four carats of diamonds, designed to slip over an Oura Ring, while The Libertine is a sterling silver pendant case adorned with diamonds and a wild-haired woman outlined in gold, designed to hold nicotine pouches or other small essentials. Equal parts extravagant and irreverent, the collection makes a playful case for enjoying life’s pleasures without sacrificing personal style.

Julia Berolzheimer’s Hart Jewelry Collection Draws on Childhood Memories

Hart is teaming up with Julia Berolzheimer for a new jewelry collection that celebrates the art of the stack. Inspired by Berolzheimer’s childhood memories of her grandmother’s California ranch and her collection of Art Deco minaudières, the collaboration brings together whimsical charms, colorful gemstones, and meaningful talismans designed to be mixed, layered, and restyled. Botanical motifs take shape in Tree of Life coins, daisies, bees, and fruit-inspired charms, while carnelian, turquoise, and pink opal add playful pops of color. One standout is the Perfume Vesta Case, a modern interpretation of a Victorian-era accessory that can hold a sample-sized fragrance and hang alongside other charms. With interchangeable chains, cords, and pendants, the collection makes a case for jewelry that feels just as personal as the memories behind it.

David Yurman Captures the Magic of a New York Holiday

David Yurman is celebrating the magic of the holidays in New York City with a new campaign featuring global brand ambassador Michael B. Jordan alongside actresses Yerin Ha and Inde Navarrette. Set against a snow-covered Washington Square Park, the campaign captures a series of quintessential New York moments, from Jordan and Ha facing off in a spirited card game to Navarrette hailing a cab in search of the perfect holiday gift. Throughout the campaign, the cast wears some of the house’s most recognizable designs, including 18-karat gold Cable bracelets and pieces from the “Starburst” and “Armory” collections. Directed by Bradford Young and photographed by Drew Vickers, the campaign brings together the spirit of the city, the joy of togetherness, and the timeless appeal of David Yurman’s jewelry.

Vhernier Reintroduces Its Iconic ‘Trottola’ Design With New Proportions

Vhernier is revisiting one of its most recognizable designs with a new interpretation of “Trottola,” the sculptural collection originally introduced in 2003. Inspired by the continuous motion of a spinning top, the latest designs play with proportions, contrasting materials, and asymmetrical shapes across rings, bracelets, necklaces, and earrings. Polished rose gold meets glossy black jet, with select pieces featuring diamond pavé for an added contrast of light and dark. The collection also focuses on versatility, from rings designed for stacking to convertible earclips that can be worn as studs or dangling earrings. With its fluid forms and unexpected material combinations, “Trottola” brings a fresh perspective to Vhernier’s signature sculptural approach to jewelry.

Di Volpe is rethinking the classic tennis bracelet with “DiSegno,” a new customizable fine jewelry system designed to change with its wearer. Using concealed, patent-pending connections, individual cultured diamonds and gemstones, called Elements, can be removed, rearranged, or added by hand, allowing wearers to transform bracelets into necklaces or earrings without compromising the seamless look of traditional tennis jewelry. The collection launches with 28 stone-and-cut combinations, including rubies, emeralds, sapphires, and diamonds, alongside a limited-edition collaboration with Lebanese artist Ali Cha’aban featuring five sculptural designs. With new cuts, colors, and artist collaborations planned for future releases, “DiSegno” makes the case for fine jewelry that’s never quite finished.

Brent Neale Riffs on the Bow in Fine Jewelry

Brent Neale is putting a bow on the holiday season with “Wrap It Up,” a new fine jewelry collection that transforms the familiar ribbon motif into sculptural works of art. Drawing inspiration from Old Hollywood glamour and the femininity of the 1960s, the designer plays with the contrast between rigid precious metals and the soft movement of fabric, crafting bows that twist, curl, and unfurl in 18-karat gold and platinum. Colored gemstones sit nestled within the ribbon-like forms, while pavé diamonds accentuate every curve and fold. Equal parts playful and precious, the collection brings a little gift-wrapped glamour to the jewelry box.

Grace Winfrey’s ‘Poppy Fortuna’ Collection Reimagines Good-Luck Charms

Grace Winfrey is bringing a little extra luck to the jewelry box with “Poppy Fortuna,” a new fine jewelry collection inspired by the natural beauty of the Italian landscape and symbols of good fortune. Scarlet poppies, sunflowers, bees, four-leaf clovers, horseshoes, and ladybugs come to life through vibrant gemstones and intricate pavé, creating miniature mosaics of color and texture. Highlights include a Lucky Bangle combining three good-luck charms, sculptural sunflower earrings with tiny ladybugs tucked into their petals, and layered charm necklaces designed to feel like modern keepsakes. Handcrafted in New York City, each piece transforms familiar symbols of prosperity, protection, and happiness into playful, colorful works of art.

Robinson Pelham Channels ’90s Glamour for Its Anniversary

Robinson Pelham is closing out its 30th anniversary celebrations with “Suite 96,” a new campaign and collection launch inspired by the glamour of late-’90s London. Set inside a private suite at St. James’s Hotel & Club in Mayfair, the campaign considers jewelry the ultimate room service, with diamonds arriving on trays, gold spilling out of wardrobes, and plenty of pieces to layer before a night out. At the center is “Studio 30,” a four-piece anniversary collection featuring diamond necklaces and statement earrings, including the sculptural Via and Hira necklaces, cascading diamond drops, and the bold Solstice Supreme. Alongside the anniversary designs, the house introduces new collections and additions to existing favorites, from chunky gold links and graphic heart rings to colorful enamel and gemstone combinations. Together, the launches celebrate three decades of Robinson Pelham’s bold, playful approach to fine jewelry.

Le Vian and Jared Revive Georgian-Era Romance

Le Vian is bringing a little old-world romance to Jared Jewelers with its new exclusive “Georgian Chocolate & Nude Diamonds” collection. Inspired by the candlelit jewels of the Georgian era, when jewelry was designed to capture and reflect the warmth of natural light, the collection rethinks historic buttercup settings in polished Honey Gold, with eight rounded prongs framing each natural diamond. The designs pair Le Vian’s signature Chocolate and Nude Diamonds with warm gold detailing across solitaire rings, anniversary bands, tennis bracelets, necklaces, and earrings. Select styles introduce colorful gemstones including Chocolate Quartz, Green Apple Peridot, and Grape Amethyst, giving the vintage-inspired silhouettes a contemporary update. With its sculptural settings and warm-toned stones, the collection brings the romance of antique jewelry into the present.

Wempe’s ‘Au:thentic’ Celebrates the Art of Goldsmithing

Wempe’s new gender-inclusive fine jewelry collection, “Au:thentic,” puts craftsmanship front and center, finding inspiration in the foundational skills taught to aspiring goldsmiths. The collection takes its shape from the jump ring, one of the first techniques Patrick Sieroslawski learned as an apprentice more than 22 years ago, translating its form to necklaces, bracelets, rings, earrings, and pendants. Handcrafted at Wempe’s atelier in Germany, the pieces come in 18-karat yellow, white, and rose gold, with select styles set with diamonds. “Au:thentic” also marks the beginning of a multiyear rollout, with three additional chapters set to expand on its design language through twists, wraps, and interlocking links.

Luckily, we've done the rummaging for you, turning up a GQ-endorsed assortment of gifts that look like you put in considerably more effort than a few clicks and two-day shipping.

The iconic Hanes Beefy-T turned 50 this year, and it's still the undisputed heavyweight champion of any dude's T-shirt drawer.

Our pick for the best underwear to buy in bulk, Calvin Klein's stretch briefs are as classic as they get. An easy gift they'll actually use.

The only thing better than a Dickies Eisenhower is a warmer Dickies Eisenhower. This lined version retains everything that makes the original a legend while offering a little extra protection against the cold.

Cashmere is one of life's great pleasures, and Naadam makes it possible to indulge without going broke.

A bomber jacket built to military spec by the brand that made it famous. 'Nuff said, really.

You could get them a fancier hoodie, but there's nothing wrong with sticking to the classics. Russell is an OG in the game, and its Dri-Power fleece hoodie is practically return-proof.

Ralph gave us the gift of the Polo Bear. Now you can give the gift of the Polo Bear on a terrific beanie.

Dress socks are one of the easiest wardrobe upgrades—and these Polo Ralph Lauren crews are cushy, classic, and primed for all the holiday shindigs filling up your calendar.

Fact: A guy can always use another polo shirt. Lacoste's iconic cotton-piqué original has the perfect combination of heft and breathability, not to mention nearly a century of good taste behind it.

Time and again, the Levi's 501 ends up right back at the top of our jeans guide. Some things never go out of style, and a great pair of straight-leg jeans is one of them.

Reebok's Club C Vintage has long been a favorite around GQ, and it might just be the best sneaker the Everything Store has to offer.

The 997H is the more affordable, everyday-minded cousin of New Balance's premium 997, with much of the same dad-shoe charm at a fraction of the price.

Merrell's Moab 3 is a tried-and-true hiking boot, and gifting a pair might be just the nudge they need to get off the couch and onto a trail.

There's no shortage of loafers out there, but Sebago makes a particularly good one.

A burly rugby from Taylor Stitch might be just what their wardrobe needs. And its clean look means pretty much anyone can rock it.

Who gifts a whole damn bar cart? From Amazon, no less? Well, Umbra makes a great one, and you don't have to tell them where you got it.

Gift them a wall sconce that doesn't require an electrician or a security deposit sacrifice. Renter-friendly lighting has rarely looked this good.

For the matcha obsessive, or the aspiring one, Fellow makes what might just be the best set out there right now.

Newgate clocks are eminently giftable, bringing a little analog charm to just about any home.

Marshall built its reputation on amps, and the Emberton III shrinks that down to size that fits in your tote bag.

Tower 28's travel-size SOS set packs everything they need to stay fresh on the go. A little skincare insurance for wherever the holidays take them.

#6710. Zara Tindall’s Little Feather Hat Makes Her Whole Look

The royal showed off her fall style at the November Meeting

Zara Tindall is back at the races. The royal made an appearance on day one of the November Meeting at Cheltenham Racecourse in Gloucestershire, England, and she brought her regal autumnal wardrobe with her.

Zara leaned into the season in shades of brown. A dark chocolate turtleneck was layered under a long L’agence coat in a burnt orange, cream, and brown houndstooth pattern. The piece had sharp shoulders and was belted at the waist

To continue the earth tones, Zara slipped on tall mahogany-brown leather boots from Fairfax & Favor, and coordinating leather gloves. She also carried Fairfax & Favor’s “Mini Kew” handbag in a similar brown hue.

Her best accessory, however, may have been her “Haya” percher hat by milliner Sally Ann Provan (of Sally Ann Hats), featuring a dark flower and a single feather.

Finally, it was her drop earrings what broke up the browns with a welcome pop of green.

Zara wore a similar look to the Cheltenham New Year’s Day races on January 1.

The royal has a long history in the equestrian world—not only as a big fan, but also as a competitor.

Zara’s parents, Princess Anne and Captain Mark Phillips, were both Olympic equestrians, and taught her to ride when she was just a toddler. As an adult, she turned the hobby into a career, following their footsteps and famously competing as part of Great Britain’s eventing team at the 2012 London Olympics, on her horse High Kingdom, where she won a team silver medal.

#6706. Ayo Edebiri Got the Forehead Curl Memo

Ayo Edebiri is one of the best-dressed people in Hollywood. In 2024, GQ named her a rising star in menswear. At our 2026 Men of the Year party, she made an even stronger case for herself as a style icon for the ages. Walking the red carpet at the Chateau Marmont in West Hollywood, the Emmy-winning actor continued her winning streak of power suiting in a navy chalk-stripe ensemble, a bright emerald-turquoise dress shirt, and a burgundy geometric tie. Her bob was styled in a side part, with a pronounced curl sweeping across her forehead. It’s a look that’s become a staple among Hollywood’s best-dressed men this year, a callback to Superman’s signature swoop, minus the Spandex tights and cape.

In the 1920s, the playful wisp of hair was known as the kiss curl: a deliberately placed lock of hair that sat on the forehead, even amid an otherwise carefully sculpted ’do. (As Seth Rogen helpfully pointed out on Instagram after we noted the kiss curl’s 2026 resurgence: “It’s called a Forelock.”) Its prominence in men’s grooming can be traced back in part to the French-American entertainer Josephine Baker, whose iconic curl ushered in an era—and now a century—of rogue forehead curls.

The kiss curl was so emblematic of the era that it made a triumphant return at the 2025 Met Gala, themed “Superfine: Tailoring Black Style.” A host of women paired the look with impeccable tailoring, including Simone Biles, Taraji P. Henson, Teyana Taylor, and, yes, Ayo Edebiri.

The modern appeal of the forehead curl is easy to understand. As hairstyles have grown longer, looser, and less structured, the curl lends an air of studied nonchalance—as if you didn’t spend too much time getting your hair just right. It’s sexy in a just-got-out-of-bed kind of way, especially when everything else—from the rest of the hair to the outfit—remains crisp, clean, and pristine.

As Edebiri once told Vogue of dressing for the red carpet: “One of the fun parts of getting to do this sort of thing is that you get to transform and be these different permutations of yourself.” At GQ’s Men of the Year party, she once again understood the assignment.

#6705. Nanofat Is Dermatologists’ Best-Kept Secret for Younger, Fresher Skin

It’s not an injectable filler, and it’s not fat transfer. It’s a secret third thing you’ll want to try.

The last few years have been unkind to our facial fat. We sliced out our buccal pads to create sunken-in, razor-sharp cheekbones. We zapped our skin with thermal devices that accidentally melted fat away in pursuit of boosting collagen. We injected our stomachs with fat-loss GLP-1 medications, leaving our faces looking hollow. Droopy. Structurally unsound. As it turns out, facial fat is critical infrastructure—not just for looking younger, but for your skin's overall health and quality. And while you can’t choose where you lose or gain fat, you can choose to have a doctor siphon it, remix it, and reinject it.

“Adipose tissue is a rich source of growth factors and progenitor cells, and re-injecting fat is probably one of the best ways to regenerate the full potential of healthy skin I've seen in the last decades,” says Patricia Ogilvie, a Munich-based dermatologist and member of the Dior Reverse Aging Board. “There are trends that are not really worth being a trend. I think the restaging of the importance of adipose tissue is very justified.”

You’re probably familiar with fat transfer, a procedure that’s been around for decades. In simple terms, fat transfer takes adipose tissue from one area of your body, like your flanks, liposuctions it, and moves it to another area, like your breasts or cheekbones. “With traditional fat transfer, it’s about restoring volume. And because it’s your own living tissue, it can integrate beautifully and give you very natural-looking results,” says dermatologist Sheerene Idriss, medical director and founder of Idriss Dermatology in New York City. “But what’s interesting is that fat isn’t just fat. It also contains regenerative cells, including adipose-derived stem cells, and growth factors that may help improve the surrounding tissue over time. Nanofat is where it gets really exciting.”

Nanofat is part of a new class of regenerative aesthetics offered by dermatologists and plastic surgeons, treatments that don’t just make you look better, but rather address the signs of aging from the inside out by stimulating collagen or repairing tissue. Imagine taking that same fat from a traditional fat transfer and processing it into a fine, milky liquid rich in your own stem cells and growth factors, then injecting or microneedling it back into your face—that’s nanofat.

“Instead of using it to restore volume, you’re using it to potentially improve skin quality itself,” says Idriss. “These cells and growth factors communicate with surrounding tissue and can stimulate processes involved in collagen production, tissue repair, and blood vessel formation. So you’re not just trying to fill a wrinkle. You’re trying to improve the skin itself—its thickness, resilience, and texture—so that wrinkle potentially becomes less noticeable.”

The best areas for nanofat injections include under the eye, a notoriously risky area for hyaluronic acid fillers, and the cheekbones. “The ideal patient for nanofat is someone who's starting to notice thinner, crepier skin, fine lines, or changes in skin texture, especially around the eyes, neck, or chest, and wants to improve skin quality rather than add volume,” adds Idriss, who both has had the treatment done and offers it in her practice. Plus, Ogilvie notes, nanofat doesn’t attract water the way fillers do, so it won’t cause under-eye puffiness (a common post-filler complaint). But because nanofat doesn’t restore volume as much as it reinvigorates your skin, you can inject it almost anywhere you’re noticing signs of aging.

“We do it under tumescent local anesthesia, so you’re awake the entire time, and recovery is usually pretty quick,” says Idriss. “I personally had nanofat and fat transfer in June and was back at work the next day. The biggest downside is some soreness at the fat extraction site, which usually lasts a few days, and you’ll want to avoid strenuous exercise for about a week. Because there’s no general anesthesia, you’re also avoiding the grogginess and recovery associated with being put under.”

Like any cosmetic treatment, it has risks and downsides. Experts note that nanofat isn’t the right treatment for anyone looking to restore significant volume loss or seeking instant results. “Improvement in skin quality can vary from person to person, and it takes months to see the full results,” Idriss adds. “There are rare but serious risks, including infection, vascular complications, and even vision loss when injecting certain areas of the face.” But patients who have tried the procedure say the recovery is quick and easy, with results compounding over weeks, though they ultimately fade away faster than traditional injectables.

Nanofat injections sit somewhere between microfat and hyaluronic acid fillers. Microfat can be lumpy and unpredictable when injected, sometimes leading to lopsided results. Plus, in any fat transfer, only a small amount of fat survives. Fillers, on the other hand, offer long-lasting precision and volume restoration, but patients are tired of looking overfilled and unnaturally plump. Nanofat helps your skin look naturally healthier, fresher, and firmer, at least for a while. After all, it’s made from you.

“I look at this as something you can do periodically throughout your life, but what you do in between treatments is just as important. And that’s why I don’t believe in demonizing any one treatment, including filler,” says Idriss. “When used appropriately, for the right indication, these treatments can all work beautifully together. It’s about knowing what you need, when you need it, and when enough is enough.”

#6702. Andrew Garfield’s Hair Is the Mane Attraction

Andrew Garfield’s hair is very long—and oh so glorious. Production ultimately put him in a wig, but Garfield kept the length regardless. And thank goodness he did. The actor brought his enviable mane to the red carpet at our annual Men of the Year party at the Chateau Marmont in Los Angeles on Thursday night, where it held its own among Hollywood’s finest.

The Artificial star arrived in an Edward Sexton suit, accessorized with a Breguet watch. But, as has been the case lately, his hair was the real headliner. The neck-grazing length was in fine form, with a few stray strands tucked neatly behind his ears. And then there was the forehead curl: a particularly on-trend flourish that’s found its place atop some of this year’s best-dressed stars (including Ayo Edebiri).

We first caught a glimpse of Garfield’s longer locks at Wimbledon this summer in London. At the time, his longtime hairstylist, Lucy Halperin, let us in on the secret to the look: a little sea salt spray, styling cream, and a diffuser to bring out his natural curls and waves. The combination enhances the hair’s volume while keeping frizz at bay.

That said, Halperin also credits his good hair to a bit of genetic luck. “Sometimes we just give it a good little wet down, and it kind of just works with him,” she told us at the time.

Whatever transformations Garfield has in store for his next on-screen role, we hope this particular look sticks around. Because if Thursday night was any indication, he’s not quite ready to part with it—and frankly, neither are we.

“This set of brushes from Anisa Beauty makes applying my base makeup a dream,” beauty commerce editor Tiffany Dodson Davis says. “Not only are the bristles super soft, but their angled shapes make it easy to blend my foundation and concealer quickly and seamlessly.”

Brushes included: Pinnacle foundation brush, angled concealer brush

What Are the Best Makeup Brushes Worth Shopping?

According to Erickson, the most essential makeup brushes in your set are the ones you use with powder products, such as bronzer, blush, or setting powder. "Everyone should own a small powder brush—or even something that resembles a large eyeshadow brush—to cut shine where needed and set concealer. An angled brush can be helpful when using bronzer or contour, as well as a medium-sized cheek brush for powder blush."

And when it comes to eye makeup brushes, the expert adds, "It can be helpful to have a dual-sided angled brush-spoolie combo for brows, as well as for winged liner. A small, dense, pointed brush for the lash line and inner corner is nice to have, as well as one or two blending brushes for the eyelids."

Should I Opt for Synthetic or Natural Bristles?

"I like to say there is nothing 'natural' about animal hair," Anisa Telwar Kaicker tells Bazaar. "It can dry faster and break more quickly. Man-made synthetics can be long-lasting, hygienic, innovative in shape, and soft to the touch."

Erickson agrees that synthetic makeup brushes outperform products made using animal by-products. "Synthetic brushes tend to be more durable and last longer. Less and less natural bristles areused today, and as a makeup artist, I don’t think we need them, performance-wise."

What’s the Most Effective Way to Clean Makeup Brushes?

"When I deep clean my makeup brushes once or twice a month, I typically use Dr. Bronner’s 18-in-1 castile soap," Erickson notes. "At the very least, use a quick-dry brush cleaner like Sephora’s Daily Brush Cleaner between each use to avoid the spread of bacteria."

Telwar Kaicker suggests that after deep cleaning, you remove excess water from your brushes with a towel. Then, tilt the brush downward to prevent water from seeping into the ferrule and breaking down the glue in the brush head.

How Often Should I Replace My Makeup Brushes?

According to Erickson, high-quality, well-cared-for brushes can last for years. "If it ain’t broke, don’t fix it. I’ve had some of my makeup brushes last a decade and some only last a year or two. If you love it and you’re able to properly sanitize it, use it for as long as you can."

How do you know when it's time for a new set? Erickson says it all comes down to the glue. "Typically, when a makeup brush goes bad, the glue between the brush and handle starts to break down due to wear and moisture from cleaning. When that happens, toss it and move on. For beauty blenders and sponges that harbor bacteria, toss them after a few uses, no matter how well you sanitize them. Toss after a few uses, especially if you’re acne-prone."

#6700. Taco Bell Made An Exclusive Hot Dog & Fans Are Freaking Out

“Imagine getting a glizzy from Taco Bell 😭”

Taco Bell is no stranger to controversial menu items, but one new viral dish might be the wildest yet.

Last week, the Tex-Mex chain launched the first-ever Live Más Open, a star-studded golf tournament hosted by Kevin Hart. The guest list for the nine-hole competition included pro athletes, television stars, musicians, and more. However, the appearance that’s generating the most buzz isn’t a celebrity—it’s a Taco Bell hot dog.

Attendees were served a lineup of event-exclusive dishes that we've never seen at the Bell before, like lemon pepper ranch-dusted chicken nuggets and pimento cheese Quesaritos. Taco Bell fans, though, have the most FOMO for the Clubhouse Street Dog.

According to Taco Bell, the dish featured an all-beef hot dog served in a puffy flatbread instead of a traditional bun. Taco Bell loaded the hot dog with charred pineapple, cotija, citrus-pickled red onions, and cilantro. The whole thing is drizzled with a Fire Piña Aioli and sour cream.

Bailey Fink from Allrecipes attended the Live Más Open and tasted the hot dog for herself. She called it “easily one of the best hot dogs I’ve ever had” from a fast-food restaurant and compared the flavor profile to a traditional Colombian hot dog (minus the potato chips).

Social media users who didn't get the chance to try the Clubhouse Street Dog, though, don't seem too convinced. “The words Taco Bell and hot dog should not be in the same sentence,” one Instagram user wrote. Another added, “If you order a hot dog from Taco Bell, you need to be on watch list…”

But if you take a look at Taco Bell's origin story, introducing hot dogs would actually bring the chain full circle. Founder Glen Bell's early restaurants served hamburgers and hot dogs before he shifted his attention to tacos. He eventually opened Taco Tia, which preceded the first Taco Bell restaurant in Downey, California.

Unfortunately, though, it appears Taco Bell won't be adding hot dogs to the menu anytime soon. “The Live Más Open menu was created exclusively for the tournament day, allowing us to showcase our Taco Bell twist on classic golf bites,” a Taco Bell representative tells Delish. “There are no current plans to bring the menu nationwide, but at Taco Bell, we never say never.”

But don't despair: Part of the golf tournament prize is the opportunity to help choose a discontinued menu item to bring back for a limited time next year. So while a Taco Bell hot dog likely isn't in our immediate future, we can still look forward to the return of an old favorite.

#6695. Laila Gohar Is Inspiring Us to Celebrate Our Own Made-Up Holidays

The artist discusses her advent calendar for The Luxury Collection and finding beauty on the subway.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

On Avenue George V in Paris, in the lobby of the Hotel Prince de Galles, is a festive installation that looks straight out of a Wes Anderson movie. It’s a pop-up fashioned to look like the counter of a vintage apothecary, with rows of cup-handled drawers lining a dark wooden wall, each numbered and labeled, with an attendant standing in front in a dark green uniform and cap. Flanking it on both sides are glass casings with Christmas trees—made from light-blue fabric and white ribbons—inside, surrounded by metallic ant figurines.

The whimsical, imaginative display is part of artist Laila Gohar’s ongoing collaboration with The Luxury Collection, the hotel group, which boasts the Prince de Galles as one of its many properties. For the holidays, Gohar curated an advent calendar with each of its 24 windows offering a peek into a different hotel in the collection, from Madrid, Kyoto, Dubai, and more. In a way, this Parisian pop-up, with set designs by Alix Bortoli, is a life-size extension of the work. Similar versions appear in The Joseph in Nashville, Tennessee, Solaz in Los Cabos, and The Laurus in Singapore.

Gohar tapped her artistic circle for the project. “When people ask me, ‘Who inspires you?’ my answer is always my friends,” she says. The advent calendar’s exterior is illustrated by New York-based Joana Avillez and fashioned to look like a hotel out of a storybook. (It’s not based on any particular one in real life, though.) “When you open it up, inside of the flaps, there are all these little vignettes,” Gohar explains to ELLE. “It’s like all these imagined little scenarios, and some of them have a little bit of humor, but it’s a little bit of a Where’s Waldo thing. It’s also kind of in the style of Richard Scarry. Do you remember those books from childhood?”

Inside each window is a chocolate from Casa Bosques—founded by designer Rafael Prieto, another one of Gohar’s pals—featuring flavors from each destination. “For example, for The Suiran in Kyoto, the chocolate featured inside has black sesame and other flavors associated with Japan and with that city,” Gohar explains.

It’s a fitting undertaking for Gohar, who first earned renown for works of art made with food and has since developed her own design studio, Gohar World. (The brand just opened up a shop on Elizabeth Street in New York.) “While I care very much about food, for me, it’s more about creating a particular feeling in a space, and that can be through lots of different mediums,” she says.

That medium could be an advent calendar full of chocolates or a historic Art Deco hotel like the Prince de Galles, with its majestic marble details and mosaic tiles. ELLE caught up with Gohar one morning in Paris to discuss her latest projects, holiday gifting, and her hosting tips.

Yeah. I think there’s something nostalgic about advent calendars and you have something to look forward to every day. What I like about it is that there’s all this excitement around it, but you also have to practice a little restraint, which as a kid, I don’t know if I really did. I would blast through all of them. My mom was like, “You have to wait!” I think a lot of people grew up with them, but adults love them too. It’s very giftable, which I thought would be good for the holidays.

I love to give gifts that feel almost like an heirloom, like something that was maybe in your family. Especially with my friends, we think about that a lot. What are we creating that can be passed down from generation to generation? What is something that is really considered, that took a lot of time to create? I love thinking about gifts through that lens.

There’s a lot of pressure around giving gifts for the holidays, and obviously the way we shop now is very online. So I like to create things that feel a little bit slower and more craft-based.

For the holidays, or just in general, I always say that people are only able to relax and have a good time in your home or around you if you’re relaxed and having a good time. I think that’s really what it comes down to. You have to set yourself up for success, and that means you’re not getting involved with a really difficult cooking project that you’re really nervous about—you’re going to be running the stove all the time. That is not good. Just figure out how to create an environment that feels relaxing for you, and therefore everyone will relax and hopefully have a good time.

Oh my God, I’ve hosted so many. I write a column for The Financial Times, “How to Spend It,” and the premise of it is made-up holidays, because I just like the idea of thinking of a random excuse to get people together. I think there’s a lot of pressure around the holidays, but I like just celebrating random everyday things. For example, throwing a party because I saw really beautiful dahlias in the market and I think we should have a dahlia party. We’re going to have a soup party because it’s the coldest night of the year, or we will have a potato party because there are new potatoes in the market and I love potatoes.

Yeah. All of those are real ones. They’re not hypothetical. And I’ve done a million random things that I just kind of make up. I think there’s a reason to celebrate obviously around the holidays, but also every day. If you take a minute, there’s always a reason to spread joy and a reason to celebrate.

Last week, I was in Dakar, Senegal, and I’m participating in a biennial that’s happening there soon. In Senegal, people have unbelievable style, and you see it in just how they carry themselves and how they put outfits together. They just have this swag, and I think it makes for really great people-watching. I was inspired by people’s sense of self and how they move, how they carry themselves, how confident they appear.

It’s for the Dakar Biennale, which is the most significant art biennial in Africa. I’m from Egypt, so it was really important for me to be there. For the project, I’ve created a tapestry carpet—it’s kind of like a quilt. I teamed up with a friend of mine, Rym Beydoun; she has a clothing brand called Super Yaya. Together we created this textile that transforms a room in the biennial into a meditation space. It’s inspired vaguely by prayer carpets. Senegal is a Muslim country, and there are a lot of different carpets there, but also all over the Muslim world.

We created 25 unique carpets in the prayer carpet size, which is small, and then we sewed them all together to create this really big composition. The idea was to create a little space of refuge. The biennial’s in this big, beautiful building, and we just wanted this little corner where people could just sit with themselves for a second and spend a little time with themselves.

I think there’s inspiration everywhere you look. It depends on how you look. But I love to notice beauty or inspiration in the least expected places. Obviously there’s tons of inspiration in museums and in films and all that, but I like to notice random accidental beauty. I’m a little embarrassed to admit this, but a thing that I do is when I’m sitting on the train in New York, I kind of look at every person and I try to find one thing that I think is beautiful about them.

It’s a fun way to pass time. I see an old man sitting on the train, and I’m like, “His hair is really good,” or something. You notice all sorts of crazy things that you never would [if you didn’t] look at the person that way.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

#6694. Popular Thanksgiving Product Recalled From Costco Shelves Over Concerning Contamination Risk

Here's what shoppers need to know ahead of the holiday.

Delish editors handpick every product we feature. We may earn commission from the links on this page.

Costco members, listen up. A popular Thanksgiving topping is being recalled over concerns about possible cleaning chemical contamination. Here's what to watch for.

Costco is recalling its Kirkland Signature Real Heavy Whipped Cream ahead of the upcoming Thanksgiving holiday. The recall covers 15-ounce cans sold between October 11 and October 31, 2026, including those purchased in three-packs.

To identify the affected product, check for item number 1777000, item code AC50, and a best-if-used-by date of April 2, 2027. The cans must also have a printed timestamp between 00:35 and 02:45.

The whipped cream was sold at Costco warehouses in 12 states: Alabama, Florida, Georgia, Iowa, Illinois, Indiana, Missouri, Mississippi, North Carolina, South Carolina, Tennessee, and Wisconsin.

Producer Alamance Foods voluntarily recalled the product after learning that one batch may contain a small amount of a cleaning chemical. According to a November 7 letter sent to Costco members, some shoppers reported a chemical smell and taste.

The company said no serious adverse health effects requiring medical care had been reported. The notice does not identify the chemical or say how it may have gotten into the whipped cream.

If your can matches the affected lot and timestamp, stop using it and return it to your local Costco for a full refund. The company's notice also includes photographs of the can and its printed code to help shoppers identify the product.

For questions or concerns, contact Alamance Foods at customer.care@alamancefood.com.

#6692. I Walked After Every Meal for Two Months, and My Digestion and Energy Levels Have Never Been Better

Experts weigh in on why sitting is the worst thing you can do after eating

It’s almost 9:00 p.m., and my work dinner in Manhattan’s SoHo neighborhood is finally coming to a close. As the people around me start to get up and call their Ubers, I head out the door to go home—on foot. After a lavish dinner, most people’s last thought is to get a brisk walk in, but for me, it’s crucial—not to hit a step count or burn calories, but as my version of a digestif, if you will.

My idea to walk after dinner came from a video I saw months ago from a TikTok nutritionist who touted a brisk 10-minute walk after meals as the key to boosting metabolism, regulating blood sugar levels, and helping your stomach digest food. My two favorite pastimes are eating and walking. I never thought the two would go hand in hand.

“Sitting briefly after eating isn’t inherently harmful, but prolonged, uninterrupted sitting can lead to a higher post-meal blood-sugar response compared with breaking it up with short walks,” says Elizabeth Sharp Edens, an internal medicine and obesity medicine physician, functional medicine practitioner, and founder of HMW Method. A 2022 meta-analysis in Sports Medicine found that light-intensity walking reduced post-meal glucose by almost 17 percent. The same study found that standing breaks after meals reduced glucose spikes by 9.5 percent on average. The TL;DR: Research says that any type of movement can improve glucose levels.

We know walking can do wonders—it can clear the mind, help you lean out, and even boost dopamine—but why is it a solution for feeling less full and avoiding afternoon crashes? “When you walk, your muscles use glucose for energy,” Edens explains. “Muscle contractions move glucose transporters called GLUT4 to the surface of muscle cells, helping draw glucose out of the bloodstream through a pathway that doesn’t depend on insulin.” Since your legs, the vehicle for walking, contain some of the biggest muscles in your body, it makes sense that walking effectively stimulates muscle contractions that move glucose transporters. “Walking breaks are a simple way to support blood sugar management while getting your steps in,” she adds.

While many rely on peptides, green powders, and “magic” supplements, walking is an easy, mindless (and free) way to improve digestion and prevent blood-sugar crashes. “Even two to five minutes after a meal can help, ideally before the glucose peak, typically 60 to 90 minutes after eating,” Kiran Krishnan, a research microbiologist, the founder and chief science officer of the Biome Learning Center, and Dose key opinion leader, adds.

I often joke after large meals that I will have to be rolled home. The good news: Walking can also reduce the overwhelming feeling of fullness. “Walking also helps the gut physically,” Krishnan says, citing a study that found that a slow walk after a meal significantly shortened the time it took the stomach to empty half its contents. “For people prone to bloating, mild [walking] cut intestinal gas retention from 45 percent to 24 percent and eased symptoms,” he adds. Plus, Krishnan says studies show reduced LDL cholesterol levels and improved liver function in those who walked after meals.

Then there’s good old gravity, says Caitlin Hosmer, a Maine-based registered dietitian and co-founder of MenoPantry. “Gravity helps too, which is part of why walking may help people who feel uncomfortably full or get reflux after meals,” she explains. “Gentle movement and staying upright help food move out of the stomach and along the digestive tract.”

Ten minutes isn’t long, but studies show it’s just as effective as a longer walk. A 2025 study published by PubMed Central found that a 10-minute walk lowered glucose measurements by 6 percent and a 30-minute walk lowered glucose levels by 5 percent, meaning just 10 minutes of walking is all you need to help reduce a post-meal glucose spike. If you can walk for 30 minutes, an hour, or even longer—that’s great. But just 10 minutes can work just as well.

What matters most is how quickly you get moving. “Glucose typically peaks 60 to 90 minutes after eating, and moving before that peak is what blunts the spike,” Hosmer says. “A walk puts your muscles to work just as glucose from the meal is flooding into the bloodstream.” At first, I questioned whether I had to walk after every meal. “Put your effort where it counts most: after your largest, most carbohydrate-rich meal,” Hosmer advises, adding that for most, that’s after dinner, but walking after all three meals is ideal.

My post-meal walks varied—some days I would walk for 30 minutes or even an hour, depending on how much time I had and where I was going next. But as I started incorporating them into my work schedule, especially on busy office days, I often had only 10 minutes to spare. When in a pinch, I would get up and walk around the office floor and, at home, do air squats, which engage the same large leg muscles as walking and can be just as effective as a post-meal walk.

It may feel strange to pencil in time to walk after every meal, but the benefits I have noticed surpass any inconvenience or awkwardness. I have fewer crashes after I eat, whereas I previously would feel lethargic after every meal. I’ve also noticed improved digestion. While this can be chalked up to a number of things (my beloved vibration plate, greens powders, or digestive enzymes), I always feel lighter and less full after a post-meal walk.

It’s also not meant to feel daunting or like a chore. “Your post-dinner walk isn’t a workout. It’s a way of helping your body handle the meal,” Hosmer says. “The one real ‘wrong way’ is skipping it because you think it has to be long or perfect. I often say something is better than nothing, and that’s especially true here. Even a few minutes of walking, started soon after you finish eating, can blunt the blood sugar rise, and it may help your digestion too.”

#6691. The 5 Best Skin Care Tools for Women Over 50 That Are Worth the Investment, According to Experts

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Give your beauty routine an upgrade with these transformative tools.

There’s no shortage of skin care tools on the market. And if you’ve ever found yourself clicking through page after page of LED masks, microcurrent devices, and sculpting gadgets, wondering which ones are actually worth the investment, you’re not alone. With so many options to choose from, I set out to find the tools best suited for mature skin, focusing on the technologies that can complement a good routine rather than overwhelm it.

After 50, skin naturally begins to change. Collagen production slows, cellular turnover decreases, and hormonal shifts can bring new concerns like dryness, sensitivity, and changes in elasticity and pigmentation. But that doesn’t mean your routine needs to get more aggressive. In fact, the experts I spoke with emphasized quite the opposite: Mature skin benefits from thoughtful stimulation, consistency, and a healthy skin barrier—not from piling on increasingly intense treatments.

“Skin doesn’t need to be punished to improve,” says celebrity master esthetician Melissa Fox. Board-certified aesthetic physician associate at Row 89, Rocio Romero, agrees, pointing out that the best device is ultimately the one you’ll actually use consistently. After all, an expensive gadget collecting dust in your bathroom cabinet isn’t doing anything for your complexion.

After consulting experts, researching the options, and testing a few myself, I narrowed the crowded field down to five tools that stood out for their ability to support mature skin. Below, shop the best devices to improve firmness and radiance while temporarily reducing puffiness and sculpting the face.

“Red light is my number one,” says Dr. Romero. The wavelengths help regenerate cells and reduce inflammation. “There are different versions, and the trick is to pick the one that fits your lifestyle, because you have to be consistent with it,” she adds. This Celluma device is amazing because it has three modes (anti-aging, acne, and pain relief), and its large panel design works on your face and across your body.

Expert review: “Celluma is one of my favorite technologies because it’s gentle, noninvasive, and easy to incorporate into a consistent routine. Red and near-infrared light can help support collagen production and improve the appearance of fine lines over time. I especially love LED for mature skin because you’re encouraging healthier-looking skin without creating unnecessary inflammation. It’s a perfect example of progressive, not aggressive.”—Dr. Melissa Fox

Microcurrent devices like Nuface’s Trinity+ work wonders for lifting, tightening, and sculpting. Dr. Rocio recommends using the device on your face, neck, chest, and under-eyes. “Especially if you have Botox or filler, there are specific areas where it works beautifully,” she adds. “The contraction of the muscle will metabolize your injectables faster.”

Expert review: “Microcurrent is one of my favorite categories for women who want to address the appearance of facial contours. It uses a very low-level electrical current, and some people notice a temporary improvement in facial definition and tone. I particularly like it for clients focused on the jawline and cheek area.”—Dr. Melissa Fox

“Lyma is a great option for women who are serious about investing in advanced at-home skin care technology,” says Dr. Melissa Fox. It uses low-level laser light rather than the heat-based resurfacing approach associated with many professional lasers. It’s particularly helpful for those concerned about fine lines, texture, and overall skin quality.

Best for: Improving skin tone and elasticity

Customer review: “If you’re willing to put in the work, this will work for you! It is one of the few products that has actually changed my skin. It does take commitment, but it’s better than going somewhere for a pricey treatment. I just do it at home while watching TV!”

“Another tool that is so simple and you have at home already is ice,” says Dr. Romero. Dr. Fox concurs, saying, “Anyone who knows me knows I’m obsessed with cold therapy. I tell my clients to ice their skin daily, and cryo sticks are one of the easiest ways to incorporate cooling into a routine.” Cryo globes are the easy, luxe, and mess-free way to enjoy the process.

Expert review: “They’re wonderful for temporarily reducing puffiness, soothing the skin, and making the face look refreshed and more sculpted. I especially love them in the morning around the jawline, cheeks, and under-eye area. They don’t replace collagen-building treatments, but the immediate cosmetic benefits are beautiful.”—Dr. Melissa Fox

“Gua sha brushes are such an underrated tool,” says Dr. Fox. “Gua sha is my go-to,” Dr. Romero agrees. Gentle, deliberate movements can help temporarily reduce facial puffiness and relax areas where you hold tension, particularly around the jaw and brow.

Expert review: “As we age, the face can look more tired simply because of fluid retention or muscle tension. Gua sha is a wonderful way to bring movement and relaxation into a routine. It’s also a beautiful self-care ritual, although it won’t permanently lift the skin or replace collagen.”—Dr. Melissa Fox

Melissa Fox, celebrity master esthetician and the founder of Flawless by Melissa Fox in Miami and West Palm Beach.

Frequency depends entirely on the technology. LED can often be used several times per week, or even daily when the device’s protocol allows it. Cooling tools can be incorporated daily, and gua shas can be used a few times a week with very gentle pressure. Microcurrent should follow the specific device’s instructions, though most recommend a few times per week as well. “My biggest advice is not to use everything at once,” says Dr. Fox. “More isn’t necessarily better, especially when skin becomes more reactive with age.” Choose two or three tools that address your concerns, stay consistent, and prioritize barrier health. Skin longevity is a marathon, not a sprint.

#6690. 3 Easy Hacks To Make Instant Mashed Potatoes WAY Better

You might prefer homemade mashed potatoes, but sometimes you just need a shortcut—and on days like that, grabbing the box is WAY easier. But while the back-of-the-box directions will yield just-fine results, a few easy hacks will give you much better results.

As a recipe developer and professional cook, I don’t often make instant mashed potatoes, but I was excited by the challenge of leveling them up—without adding a bunch of extra ingredients or steps that take the convenience out of this convenience food. So I tried making instant mashed potatoes every way I could think of (including the way the box says!). In the end, I found three tricks that, while super simple, massively improve that final bowl of mashed potatoes.

Here are three ways to instantly upgrade instant mashed potatoes.

Most boxes tell you to rehydrate instant mashed potato flakes in hot water enriched with a little butter and a few tablespoons of milk—but I’m going all in on the milk here. The extra dairy really fills out the flavor of the mashed potato and makes it creamier—especially if you’re using a higher-fat milk, like whole or 2%.

When swapping milk for water, it’s best to increase the liquid amount just slightly. For some reason (totally scientific, I’m sure!), the potato flakes require more milk than water to hydrate properly. I recommend 2 extra tablespoons for every half cup of instant mashed potatoes.

Also, add the extra milk the box typically calls for. If you leave it out, the potatoes will be dry. When I was testing, I found it didn’t really matter when that second amount of milk went into the pan (at the beginning versus just before the potatoes), but some boxes emphasize putting it in cold just before adding the potatoes—so if you want to do that to make you feel safer, be my guest!

All the instant mashed potatoes I made lacked seasoning—until I doubled the salt. Then they were perfect. Now here’s the thing: I was testing with Diamond Crystal kosher salt, which is less salty by volume than table salt or Morton’s kosher. The back of the instant mashed potato box didn’t specify what type of salt they used, so if they tested with a fine salt or Morton’s kosher, maybe ¼ teaspoon was the perfect amount. But in my kitchen with Diamond Crystal, it was woefully underseasoned.

Maybe you’re nervous about oversalting and don’t want to double or even slightly increase the salt right away. But regardless, I’m begging you: Taste those potatoes before you serve them and don’t feel bad if you have to add another hefty pinch.

You might assume that mashed potatoes should be made in a pot—I definitely did. But the fluffiest, creamiest instant potatoes I made in this whole testing process came from a wide, high-sided sauté pan. The reason for this? Absolute science.

When adding the instant potato flakes to the hot liquid, the goal is to distribute them as evenly as possible without working them too much. Yes, the back of the box says to “stir” the potatoes in, but in testing, I quickly discovered that even a few strokes can quickly lead to gummy potatoes.

Here’s where the pan size comes in. Using a wide pan increases the liquid's surface area, so you can sprinkle the potatoes evenly over the top and pat them down into the liquid instead of stirring. From there, let them stand until they’ve absorbed the liquid, then give them a few stirs. Trust me: They’ll be way fluffier because you messed with them less!
